Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (the spinning Earth; the Sun at the centre and its eight planets; asteroids and comets; to scale; how we found out), in the lesson's own words and with its own pictures: its day and night sim (ART.sim dayNight 0-3, the drawing its Spin button steps through), the eight planet pics of its order step, the rock of its asteroid card, and the football, peppercorn, grape and pea of its scale demo.
title: The Solar System
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Explain why the spinning of the Earth on its axis leads to the apparent movement of the Sun, night and day, and changes in shadows.
Name the planets in the Solar System.
Know that the Sun is at the centre of the Solar System.
Know that planetary systems can contain stars, planets, asteroids and comets.
Use models to show relationships, quantities or scale.
Describe how scientific knowledge and understanding changes over time through the use of evidence gained by enquiry.

beats.say: The Sun does not cross the sky. The Earth spins, and carries you round.
Round the Sun go eight planets, a belt of rock, and comets made of ice.
The Earth spins once every twenty-four hours. One spin, one day.
It spins on its axis: an imaginary line through the middle, pole to pole.
When your side faces the Sun it is day. At midday the Sun looks high.
Turn a quarter further and the Sun looks low. Sunset.
Another quarter and your side faces away. Night. The Sun did not move. You did.
The spin swings your shadow round, and changes its length.
The Sun is a star: a huge ball of hot, glowing gas.
It sits at the centre of the Solar System, and eight planets go round it.
Nearest is Mercury. Then Venus, then Earth, then Mars.
Those four are small and rocky. Earth is third, not first.
Further out come the giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Jupiter is the biggest. Saturn has the great rings, and Neptune is farthest out.
Between Mars and Jupiter is a belt of rocks called asteroids.
An asteroid can be as small as a house, or hundreds of kilometres across.
From the cold edge of the Solar System come comets: balls of ice and dust.
Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, streaming out as a glowing tail.
A comet is not a shooting star. It goes round the Sun, far out in space.
A star, planets, asteroids and comets: that is a planetary system.
Pictures squeeze the planets together so they fit on the page.
A scale model shrinks everything by the same amount: sizes and distances.
Let the Sun be a football, about twenty centimetres across.
Then the Earth is a peppercorn, twenty-five metres away.
Jupiter is a grape, a hundred and thirty metres off.
Neptune is a small pea, seven hundred and fifty metres away: most of a kilometre.
For two thousand years people put the Earth at the centre.
It matched what you see. The Sun rises, crosses the sky and sets.
Then Copernicus did the sums. They fitted better with the Sun at the centre.
Galileo's telescope saw four moons going round Jupiter.
He saw Venus change phase too. Not everything went round the Earth.
The evidence won. Knowledge changes when enquiry brings evidence.
The Earth spins, so the Sun only seems to move, and day turns into night.
Eight planets go round the Sun, with asteroids and comets too.
A scale model keeps sizes and distances true. Evidence put the Sun at the centre.
